text.text: Background: Most individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) exhibit sensory challenges in daily life.
Findings regarding temporal information processing in autism have been inconsistent.
The association between subjective or caregiver-reported sensory abnormality and impaired time sensitivity in autism is still unclear.
Objective: The aim of this systematic review is to synthesize the evidence of the relationship between sensory features and time perception in autistic individuals.
We searched the literature databases of PubMed, Scopus, and PsycINFO by using terms relevant to autism, time perception, and sensory feature.

We excluded reports that used no comparison groups, that set no experimental condition to examine the change of response to a time, and that did not assess self-or parent/caregiver-reported sensory features.
We checked the quality of the included studies by using checklists relevant to the individual article types.
We summarized the results of group differences of sensory abnormality and time sensitivity and/or correlations between these indices and synthesized the findings based on the study characteristics.
Results: The database searches detected 773 titles, and we finally included 20 articles after screening.
Seventeen quantitative research articles that met the inclusion criteria included a total of 1,136 participants (503 autistic individuals and 633 controls).

Most reported heightened sensory abnormalities in autism, but a majority of the studies showed comparable time sensitivity examined by behavioral, neural, and physiological measures relative to controls.
The included narrative reviews discussed the potential association between the sensory abnormality and poor temporal processing in autism.
However, synthesized findings from the experimental studies indicated that no study reported an association between sensory abnormality and reduced sensitivity to time.
Reported correlations between sensory abnormality and time sensitivity were inconsistent.
In contrast to the prevailing narrative of poor temporal processing in individuals with autism, its linkage with sensory features is not evident.
Some studies displayed inappropriate use of sensory assessment tools that may also be a limitation of the present findings.
The brain organizes sensory information to create our perception of time.

Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder, and 90% of autistic individuals may have altered sensory experiences, including sensory hyper-or hyporesponsiveness and seeking behavior [1].

text.text: Such neurophysiological alternation is expected to affect a variety of information processing, including time perception.

The existence of a tight relationship between the dynamics of brain metabolites and temporal information processing has been broadly accepted, and thus temporal distortion in disorders and diseases relevant to neurotransmitters is frequently suggested [8].

text.text: However, previous systematic reviews have reported mixed findings regarding temporal processing differences between autistic and non-autistic individuals [9, 10].

text.text: A systematic review examined the alternation of temporal information processing in autism based on three types of experimental tasks: time sensitivity, interval timing, and higherorder time perception [9].

text.text: According to this article, there are inconsistent findings regarding group-level differences in performance of these task types among the 46 included studies.
The discrepancy is especially evident in studies that used simple demand; for example, a discrimination task for durations between two beeps.
In contrast, task performance demanding the cognitive function of prospective memory such as "we will lunch in five minutes" were consistently worse in autistic cohorts.
This suggests that group differences in tasks may be enhanced by the cognitive demands or complexities of information, rather than by temporal information processing itself.
Another meta-analysis examined the performance of timing tasks in individuals with autism or dyslexia [10].
text.formatted: Another meta-analysis examined the performance of timing tasks in individuals with autism or dyslexia <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: This review focused on studies using temporal order judgment (TOJ) and simultaneity (synchrony) judgment (SJ) tasks and analyzed the findings according to unisensory and multisensory domains.
For these tasks, subjects received two unisensory or multisensory stimuli with synchronous or asynchronous intervals ranging from milliseconds to supraseconds (stimulus onset asynchrony [SOA]).
text.formatted: For these tasks, subjects received two unisensory or multisensory stimuli with synchronous or asynchronous intervals ranging from milliseconds to supraseconds (stimulus onset asynchrony <ref type="bibr">[SOA]</ref>).

text.text: In the TOJ tasks, subjects were required to answer which stimulus occurred earlier or later, whereas, in the SJ tasks, subjects had to report whether the stimuli were presented synchronously or asynchronously.
The temporal thresholds of these tasks were calculated based on a sufficient time interval to correctly answer.
In the review, 18 studies on autistic individuals and 13 studies on dyslexic individuals were included in the meta-analysis.
Overall, the authors found a moderate effect of poorer sensitivity to time interval in autistic individuals compared with controls.
The effect was very small in unisensory studies but moderate in multisensory studies, although this difference in effect was not significant.

Summarizing the two evidence syntheses, group-level difference seemed to be derived from information complexity, such as the involvement of other cognitive function or the number of sensory modalities, rather than temporal processing itself.

Considering the sophisticated heterogeneity of sensory features in autism, it is not surprising that temporal processing of sensory stimuli may not differ from that in non-autistic individuals at a group level.
Rather, it is important to elucidate how temporal processing characteristics relate to daily sensory challenges in autism.

In this review, we synthesized findings examining the associations between timing tasks and sensory symptoms that are clinically or subjectively assessed from the perspective of autistic individuals and their caregivers.
The aim of this systematic review was to elucidate the relationship between sensory features and time perception in individuals with autism.

Since time perception should assume the specific biological response to temporal differences, any studies that examined behavioral, neural, and physiological measures were deemed eligible for the review.
We followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses
We designed a search strategy based on the PICO framework to ensure the validity, applicability, and completeness of the systematic review.
We defined "Patient" as ASD, "Intervention" as sensory symptom, "Comparison" as normal sensation, and "Outcome" as performance of the time perception task.
Search terms were related to autism, time perception, and sensory hyperresponsiveness.

text.text: The quality of each study included in our review was assessed using checklists; the Kmet checklist (QUALSYST, [13]) was used for research reports, including theses, and the Scale for the Quality Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) [14] was used for narrative reviews.

text.text: The Kmet checklist for quantitative studies comprises 14 items and each study was scored in terms of the degree to which it met the criterion of each item ("yes" = 2, "partial" = 1, "no" = 0).
Items considered as not applicable to the quality assessment were excluded from the calculation of total score.
The SANRA checklist includes six items, ranked on a scale from 0 to 2, where a higher number indicates higher quality.

text.text: This assessment comprises eight items addressing participant eligibility and characteristics, measurement of exposures and outcomes, identification and management of confounding factors, and statistical analysis.
Each item is rated as "Yes," "No," "Unclear," or "Not applicable," based on the information reported in the study.
Rather than applying a universal numerical cutoff, item-level judgments are used to identify potential sources of bias.
The risk of bias assessment was performed by two authors (T.A. and M.I.) independently.

Quantitative studies were coded into four categories: experiments measuring behavioral indices for time sensitivity; brain responses using, for example, electroencephalogram (EEG) and magnetoencephalogram (MEG); physiological indices such as pupillary response; and both behavioral and brain response using, for example, event-related potential (ERP) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).
To examine associations between performance on timing tasks and sensory features in autism, we prioritized findings based on correlational analyses in clinical groups.
If correlational analyses were not performed in the study, we checked the differences of indices between groups and estimated the group-level association between metrics of interest.
If there was a statistical value in the study, we reported the effect size of group differences and correlations, based on Cohen's d and correlation coefficients, respectively.
If no effect size value was given but mean and standard deviation (SD) were reported in the text, we calculated Cohen's d.
If an article reported the effect size, mean, and SD but not the 95% confidence interval (CI), we calculated the CI.

The narrative reviews included in this study were summarized to identify the theoretical arguments linking temporal processing to sensory features in autism and to compare these arguments with the empirical findings.
These narrative reviews were considered separately from the experimental studies and were not used to draw conclusions about correlations between temporal processing and sensory features.
They were not assigned statistical weights.
Our search of electronic databases initially identified 773 titles.
After screening the titles and abstracts, 667 were excluded, leaving 106 articles.
Forty duplicated articles were removed, and the remaining 66 articles were then retrieved in full.
Forty-eight articles were excluded after full article review because they did not fulfill the inclusion criteria of Reasons 1 to 3.
We found 1 further duplication and 1 study that did not include autistic individuals, leaving 18 articles.
The reference lists of these articles were then manually examined for suitable additional studies, which identified 3 articles; a manual search found 1 further article.
We screened these 4 articles and excluded 2 of them.

The authors reported that children with autism and those with autism and ADHD showed higher scores of sensory assessments compositing the SEQ and Sensory Processing Measure (SPM).
The authors also reported correlational analyses across all children and showed that there was no association between the TOJ threshold and sensory scores.

Most of these scores of assessments from autistic individuals were higher than those of neurotypical children, except Sensation seeking.
The GD threshold in autistic children was higher than that of their peers, but correlation analyses were not performed.

They found higher thresholds in autistic children than in controls, regardless of the child's dominant hand (right hand: d = 0.83, CI = [0.3, 1.35]; left hand: 0.7, [0.18, 1.23], and dominant hand: 0.64, [0.12, 1.16]) but no correlations (rs ≤ ± 0.2).

There were no correlations between the tactile or sensitivity index and task performance.

The authors assessed sensory traits in each of 19 autistic and control participants by using Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ), extracting item #5 regarding auditory ("I often notice small sounds when others do not").

None of the reviews cited empirical evidence of an association between sensory challenges and time sensitivity in autism.
Despite the existing narrative reviews, it remains unclear whether the deficits in temporal information processing are associated with increased abnormality of daily sensory experiences in autism.

text.text: Because our systematic review does not include enough studies with tasks that demand different mechanisms, it is not possible to conclude whether a single or multiple clock theory can explain the inconsistencies in the studies.
In the present study, the included studies were highly heterogeneous.
We intended to perform a comprehensive review by minimizing the likelihood of arbitrarily excluding relevant studies.
However, this strategy can result in large variability of study characteristics.

Despite this strategy, only a small number of studies was included, suggesting that empirical research connecting the academic interest in temporal processing to the everyday sensory difficulties in autism is still in its infancy.
We found five studies in which single correlational analyses were performed between sensory features and time sensitivity indices in an autistic cohort.
Two of the studies involved children [19, 29], and three involved adults [18, 27, 30].

text.text: These studies used single or multiple sensory domains and a variety of experimental tasks and sensory assessment instruments.
Including these study characteristics, the confounds of age, IQ, ADHD comorbidity, and medication were not examined in our analyses.

The risk of bias analysis also revealed that the majority of studies did not address confounding factors; therefore, we cannot exclude the possibility that these factors biased the synthesized results.
The small number of studies for each confound prevents us from establishing a generalizable relationship between sensory features and temporal processing in autism.
Another limitation of our study was that the protocol of this review was not prospectively registered due to time constraints.

The lack of prospective registration makes it difficult to verify that the review methods were prespecified and to assess whether the eligibility criteria, outcomes, or synthesis methods changed in response to the findings.
While this does not prove selective reporting, it reduces methodological transparency.
It should be acknowledged that our systematic review might have missed relevant literature.

We selected the PubMed, Scopus, and PsycINFO databases because they are advantageous for identifying literature in medical, psychological, and interdisciplinary research areas and are accessible through our institutional network.
Furthermore, we defined eligible articles as those written in English, so other possible articles of interest might have been missed.

In our systematic review, we examined associations between sensory features in autism and sensitivity in timing tasks.
Despite the prevailing narrative of poor temporal processing in autism, we found that most studies reported comparable time sensitivity between autistic and nonautistic individuals.
No study reported a correlation between enhancement of sensory abnormalities and poor time sensitivity.
However, the absence of supporting evidence should not be interpreted as evidence that no association exists between sensory features and time sensitivity.
